Critical second-opinion review of the fun core (Q10)

Add the critical second-opinion review of the fun core (Q10)

At Lukas's request, an independent read-only review tested the design
discussion before anything is built. Main findings:
- the hourly hunger rule cannot be seen at the planned clock;
- the toy no longer tests the vision's own claim that cannibalisation
  is fun;
- the toy as scoped tests five systems at once;
- a fixed-price backbone is a dominant strategy;
- "lines to towns" is a grid owner's fantasy, not a producer's;
- playtest 1 measured a quarter of the design on a tuning cliff.

The review also compares alternative cores (a season bet, the price
curve as the board, customers instead of towns) and draws lessons on
realism and fun from Hearts of Iron IV, Football Manager, Frostpunk,
Anno, Kerbal Space Program, Two Point and Cities: Skylines.

Its six questions for Lukas and its proposed changes to the toy are
recorded as Q10; Q9 is on hold for them. The toy task must be rewritten
from his answers before it starts. Tests: 110 passed.

Explorer: newest request wins, payload-only rendering, honest captions, robust inputs

Fixes QA M1, M2, m1-m13, c1-c5 and the first-impression notes.

- M1: control changes coalesced (250 ms); requests carry a generation id;
  a cooperative Scheduler (protocol.ts, shared by the worker and the
  in-page fallback) keeps only the newest request per kind, runs year >
  solar curve > long run, steps one simulated year at a time and stops a
  superseded long run at the next year boundary (cached years resume).
  Status line describes the user's current request first.
- M2: the solar slider requests only the year; summary, charts and the
  "Now" dot are drawn only from their own payload's zone/year/seed/solar.
- m1 busy indicator per request kind; m3 solar curve before the long run;
  m8 long-run charts are the baseline (captions), capture axes unbounded
  with gaps for null; m2/m6 offers chart clipped, partly-run blocks drawn
  partly solid, a note says what set the price (local offer, coupled
  neighbour, storage, regulated tariff); m7 captions (imports, flat tariffs,
  only existing neighbours/reservoirs); m4 short daily week labels; m5
  wrapping legends with room above the plot; m9 seed text field, digits
  0..4294967295 only, visible message, "Weather variation (seed)" + hint,
  URLs round-trip; m10 worker ready handshake (8 s), error event or silence
  -> in-page scheduler with a notice; m11 hashchange, #solar rounded to the
  slider step, empty/non-integer values ignored; m12 week/hour redraw only
  their charts; m13 44 px controls and larger thumbs below 600 px.
- c1-c5: labels in a note, round axis limits, value-axis duration chart
  with a rank tooltip, consistent rounding, "net imports", small fleets in
  MW, units in tooltips, 52 week steps with the last = the final 7 days.
- Titles name zone and year (and week/hour); the capture rate is dashed on
  its own right axis.

Chromium (Playwright), latest choice on screen, before -> after (laptop/phone):
5 zone changes 55.9 s -> 1.6/1.5 s; 10 x New seed 116 s -> 1.5/1.4 s;
15 x Year arrow 35 s -> 1.7/1.7 s; 8 solar keys 87 s -> 1.4/1.4 s; year
change during load 13.1 s -> 1.0/1.0 s; M2 summary after slider release
~12 s -> 1.0 s with no mixed values. No horizontal scroll at 320-1920 px,
no console errors.

Tests: scheduler supersession/priority/resume, seed parsing, week steps,
titles/captions/notes, capture axis, rounding.

Fun first (D17): propose the "power network" fun core (Q9)

Lukas, after playtest 1: hold off on realism, his feature ideas were
examples, and the game needs a fun, rewarding, engaging core inspired
by Transport Tycoon, Sid Meier's Railroads!, OpenTTD, Factorio and RTS
games. That is recorded as D17, and Q8 ("running the company") is set
aside as an idea bank.

docs/design/fun-core.md draws eight principles from those games (plus
Mini Metro) and scores slice 1 against them: it fails six of eight. It
proposes "build a power network on a living map":
- place generation on fogged spots and draw lines to towns;
- a town pays more the hungrier it is, and flooded towns pay almost
  nothing;
- power flows visibly and "+EUR" pops at the towns;
- congestion, flooding and the evening gap are self-made problems;
- towns grow when kept lit;
- Nordhav races for spots, and contracts and patents are auctioned;
- each year the player picks one of three bonuses;
- chapters with medals.

The design also lists the alternatives and how a small toy tests the
core before anything else is built. Q9 asks Lukas to approve the toy.
tasks/2026-10-04-fun-core-toy.md is ready for a yes. The roadmap, the
Phase 2 task (slices paused), the vision header and the CLAUDE.md

Analyse playtest 1 and propose "running the company" (Q8)

Lukas played slice 1: "not fun yet". He found it passive, waiting for
cash with nothing to manage, and wants per-asset stats after debt,
ways to manage assets, offshore wind, and expensive setups within
reach.

The review records his words and measures the slice 1 economy with
the stock headless runner on placeholder data. The cautious bot stops
building in 2003 on both seeds. The leveraged bot reaches bronze on
one seed and ends negative on the other. The first turbine's net cash
buys the next one about 5.5 minutes later at x1. It names five root
causes: equity is the only bottleneck, there is no operating loop, the
strategy is one-dimensional, there are no per-asset results, and the
real capital tools are missing. It maps each of his points against the
plan.

The proposed design (docs/design/running-the-company.md) adds:
- a per-asset ledger after interest;
- maintenance plans, faults, repairs and rules;
- upgrades, including price shutdown, and insurance;
- service bases and departments;
- site character and measurement campaigns;
- co-op shares, project finance, partners, and build-to-sell at an
  honest price;
- a quarterly review and a slower clock;
- charters, and offshore (the Horns Rev 1 stake, Anholt and Horns Rev
  3 tenders).

It proposes a new slice order, risks and bot targets. Q8 asks Lukas to
adopt it. Slice 2 waits on the answer. Tests: 110 passed.

Core fixes: capture-rate guard, demand streams, engine sizing, storage gap, validation, smooth fuels

Fixes stress F4, F5, F6, F8, F9, F10, F16 (rest) and analyst B3, B7.

- F4: captureRate is null when the mean price is <= 1 EUR/MWh
  (CAPTURE_RATE_MIN_MEAN_PRICE).
- F5: demand-noise stream id = hashString(zone.id) (FNV-1a + mix32), so
  DK1/DK2/DXX/SE1-4/NO1-5 get different noise.
- F6: World sizes the ClearingEngine from the technologies (39 blocks and
  2 charges per zone). 40 unlinked zones run (3.8 s/yr); chains not
  optimised (F14).
- F8: discharge bid >= charge bid + minimum spread at every price level,
  applied after the floor clamp; no same-hour charge and discharge.
- F9: addCapacity checks fromYear (integer in the inputs' range, default
  firstYear), size (finite, >= 0, cumulative <= 1e7 MW), hydro_res only with
  a reservoir, hydro_ror only with a profile (inflow series or own fleet).
- F10: validator range checks (shares, AR coefficients in [0,1), non-negative
  demand/capacity/links/fuels/reservoir/inflow, amplitudes within +-1,
  must-run overrides, reserveFraction, water-value slope 0..50,
  efficiencies, correlations); parseDate rejects days a month lacks.
- F16: shifted two-pass stdPrice (flat price -> exactly 0); normaliseMean
  iterates so the mean after the 0.98 wind clip matches the target.
- B3: the storage price window uses the computed market price.
- B7: Norway's target fill interpolated daily (dailyFromMonthly); fuel and
  CO2 follow annualPath (continuous at New Year, mean-preserving, never
  negative), replacing blendAnnual; efficiency read at the same time.

Golden hash (seed 42, 2019) 8ff7768adee91c59 -> e0003bc8c6be7e77: the demand
noise is re-seeded per full zone id (F5), storage bids keep a gap (F8),
wind is renormalised after clipping (F16), storage reads computed prices
(B3) and fuel/carbon/target fill move daily (B7). Long-run means move by
up to 2.6 EUR/MWh in Norway's low-price years; DE within 0.5.

inputs (24 F10 mutations, annualPath), weather (F5, F16), world (F4, F6,

World state: explicit snapshot/restore contract, year and seed checks, empty new storage

Fixes stress F3/F12/F15, analyst B6 and QA M3.

- WorldState + World.snapshot()/restore(): reservoir levels, storage state
  of charge and both price windows (storage thresholds, water-value anchor)
  as plain JSON-safe data, validated on restore. Contract in the world.ts
  header: a year is a pure function of inputs, seed, year and starting
  state; replaying from 1995 reproduces the long run. RollingMean now sums
  its window afresh (path-independent), windows normalise -0.
- F15: new storage starts empty; energy above a shrunken capacity is dropped
  at 1 January; storage that disappears loses its charge.
- F12: simulateYear rejects non-integer years and years outside the inputs'
  range, now explicit in the data (zones.json "years": [1995, 2025] ->
  WorldInputs.firstYear/lastYear). Seeds must be integers in 0..4294967295
  and are rejected otherwise instead of wrapped (seed >>> 0 removed).
- Explorer protocol: requests carry a generation id (gen). The long run is
  the per-seed baseline (no slider solar), cached in the worker, and
  records the state at each 1 January. Year views and the solar curve start
  from that state once it exists (payload.start = 'long-run'), so the
  summary matches the long-run charts; before that they start fresh, are
  marked provisional on the page and are recomputed when the long run gets
  there. Zone changes no longer restart the long run; a stopped long run
  resumes from its cache.

Golden hash (seed 42, 2019) f760731eca2d0449 -> 8ff7768adee91c59: storage
now starts empty instead of half full (DE pumped hydro and batteries), and
the water-value anchor mean is summed afresh (last-bit rounding). Median
speed 447 ms per year (was 411).

Tests: snapshot -> JSON -> restore -> identical hashes, F3 repro, restore
validation, F15 empty start and clamp, F12 year/seed rejection, explorer
year view = long-run stats after the long run passes the year.

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01W2M98pABuftcQaNSZaHfBb

Market clearing: fix transit throttling, scarcity spikes, empty zones, floors

Fixes the market-clearing findings of the 2026-10-04 stress test:

- F1: drop the per-zone importerRoom cap. Fixed links store a direction and
  are re-applied at full capacity on every pass; only a group that cannot
  absorb its imports at all (firm demand + exports + eligible storage
  charging) is scaled down. Transit and imports for storage charging are no
  longer throttled.
- F2: scarcity is computed per zone, once per hour, before clearing, from
  the zone's own demand (exports are not firm) and its spare capacity (own
  offers plus what each link can bring in from the neighbour's own spare).
  The lifted bids no longer depend on the grouping, so merged and split
  groups price consistently. The wrong-way repair releases a link up to
  three times per hour, largest mismatch first, instead of once.
  Wrong-way link-hours in the stress worlds: 101/68/202/26/32/20/85 -> 0.
- F7: a group with no offers and no demand prices at 0, not the cap.
- F13: one price per coupled group, held inside the highest floor and lowest
  cap; offers dispatch by their own bids; charges below the group floor do
  not buy.
- F11: addBlock/addCharge/setLinks and per-zone demand/floor/cap/reserve
  inputs throw clear errors on NaN, infinities, negative sizes, unknown
  zones and self-links.
- F16 (part): congested = fixed and prices differ (engine and LinkYear).

Engine buffers default to 64 blocks and 8 charges per zone.

Golden hash (seed 42, 2019) 18e65696d6daa883 -> f760731eca2d0449: F1 changes
dispatch and flows in the 178 link-hours where DK1-NO was throttled to DK1's
own demand; scarcity never binds in that year. Annual means 1995-2025 move
by <= 0.11 EUR/MWh except NO 2005 seed 1 (+0.7).

Regression tests from the report's reproductions (market, property with
meshed/storage/mixed-floor fuzz, world-level F1/F2); sanity wrong-way bound
tightened to 2 per year.

Analyse the end goal, competition and progression (Q7)

Lukas asked whether the goal should be taking over the whole market or
making it fully renewable, how rivals should make competition fun, and
how progression should work, compared with other market and tycoon
games.

The review compares Offworld, Capitalism Lab, Railway Empire, Anno
1800, Imagine Earth, the Patrician series, Turmoil, Power Grid and CO2.
It recommends "lead the transition": be number one by value and
renewable output against three named rivals that race for sites, grid
room and tenders. A competition-authority share cap per zone, anchored
on the 2006 DONG/Elsam remedy (about 2,400 MW sold to Vattenfall),
pushes growth abroad, and a rank ladder continues D14's levels. A fully
renewable Europe becomes the sandbox's shared goal, and takeovers stay
later (D9). Options B (take over everything) and C (mission first) are
laid out as Q7. Phase 1 and the prototype are unaffected under every
option. Tests: 77 passed.

Build the Phase 1 simulation core on placeholder inputs

A pure TypeScript simulation module (src/sim): seeded sfc32 PRNG with
saveable state, a pure calendar on a fixed one-hour timestep, validated
data inputs, a synthetic weather placeholder behind a WeatherSource
interface (daily AR(1) persistence, cross-zone correlation, seasonal
hydro inflow), an hourly demand shape, and market clearing by merged
merit order with congestion splitting, a cubic scarcity adder, negative
renewable bids, reservoir water values anchored to neighbour prices and
rule-based storage bidding into the same stack. Annual statistics
include capture prices and rates per technology.

Four zones (DK1, DE, NO, ES) and three links on placeholder data under
data/placeholder, every file marked "placeholder, unverified" and
registered in docs/licences.md as invented values.

Tests: hand-checked merit-order and coupling cases, fast-check
properties (zero-cost supply never raises a price, link limits, energy
balance), full-year invariants, storage and hydro bounds, determinism
with a golden hash, an import-boundary scan, qualitative sanity checks
and a speed measurement (about 0.5 s per simulated year, four zones).
CI runs typecheck, tests and the build with GitHub's own actions.
